utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution Douglas Stringer, Matthew Gillett, Thomas Laugel, and Kai Leung.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Bilic. I would remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when we left off we were discussing the United Nations report which is 65 ter 5499, and you have already explained that the bodies mentioned at paragraph 348, at Velepromet, are the same ones that you discussed earlier that were moved to the new cemetery in Vukovar. So that answers my final question on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLET
utterances.text: And at this stage we'd tender that 65 ter document 5499, which is the United Nations report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 5499 shall be assigned Exhibit P1513, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, my final question, Ms. Bilic, in your expert report at section 15, you describe mass graves as places where three or more victims are illegally buried without markings or measures or respect for the remains. In the report you then also go on to talk about people exhumed from individual graves, and I'm wondering, what were these individual graves like typically?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to individual graves, we're talking about places from which the mortal remains of one or two persons were exhumed. In a majority of those cases, those places were not marked as places of burial. Also, there was no documentation about the persons whose mortal remains were buried in those individual graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, those -- that completes my questions on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic for cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, are Ms. Bilic. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I represent Goran Hadzic in these proceedings. I have a few questions about your report, which is P1490. We'll start with chapter 1. In that report you say that in 1991 a commission was set up for dealing with people who were taken prisoner of war during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that -- that commission in 1993 merged with the other commission and formed a new commission for detainees and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the way I understand from your CV, it seems that in 1993, you joined the work of that commission which subsequently changed names and finally was given the name that it nowadays bears.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell me, please, according to the definition of the commission that I mentioned first, who did that commission consider a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detainees or prisoners of wars were those persons who were detained during the homeland war, i.e., those persons who were in prisons, camps, and detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say in prisons, camps, and other such places, do you also imply, do you also comprise such prisons and detention camps in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aforementioned commission primarily dealt with the exchanges of prisoners, which means that within the purview of that commission, there were also exchanges of those persons who were detained at holding centres in the Republic of Croatia as well as those who were kept in prisons and detention camps in the previously occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the commission was also an institution that had authority in the non-occupied part of the Republic of Croatia where detainees had been kept by the Croatian armed forces during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, the main task of that commission was to organise exchanges of prisoners on both sides. At this moment I don't have in front of me the decree on the setting up and the purview of the commission, so I'm not sure whether the commission was authorised to control the treatment of prisoners of war in the prisons and holding centres in the Republic of Croatia. However, I know for a fact that the commission did not keep records of those persons who were under the authority of the Republic of Croatia in respect of the armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the commission carry out searches of persons who were considered prisoners of war and of whom it was thought that they were kept in such prisons?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the purview of -- of the commission for searching missing persons. The other commissions that -- the second commission that you mentioned at the beginning. In 1993 those two commissions were merged, and they continued functioning as one body which became a commission of the government of Croatia for missing persons and now -- and nowadays this is the administration for missing and detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, you personally, were you involved in the problem of searching for persons who went missing and who may have been detained in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1993 when I started dealing with these tasks, I was involved in all of the tasks that had to do with the searches for missing persons, including such persons for which there was some indicia that they may have gone missing in the territory of the Republic of Croatia irrespective of where that may have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That means even those that may have been captured by the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would have included them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me within the framework of your tasks and duties, did you communicate, did you visit prisons and other such places where such persons were detained?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never visited prisons or any other places where prisoners of war were accommodated or detained. Prisons and similar places and supervision thereof was carried out by the International Commission of the Red Cross in the Republic of Croatia which had such a mandate. They identified the situation, and they reported to the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you, the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons communicated with the prisons in Croatia, or as you call it, the non-occupied part of Croatia, only through that international organisation and not directly.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons did not communicate with prisons and holding centres individually. It communicated with the authorised administration in the Ministry of Justice which had authority over prisons; i.e., with the Ministry of Defence which had authority over holding centres for prisoners of war. The Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons did not have any contacts nor did it have the need to communicate with prisons and holding centres. As I've already told you, it was the committee of the Red Cross that supervised the treatment of prisoners of war in such facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In chapter 2, you spoke about the authorities and competencies of the administration. You mentioned all of those territorial authorities, and I noticed that one of them were exhumations and identifications of mortal remains. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have read all of the decisions that concern the organisation and jurisdiction of the commission from 1991 onwards, and I noticed that one thing missing and that's autopsies. That was never part of the commission's jurisdiction. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, we're talking about a very professional work that is carried out by competent scientific institutions on behalf of the administration. The administration for detainees and missing signed an agreement with competent scientific and medical institutions which then carry out that part of expert activities on behalf of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with your position that this is a very highly specialised activity. However, it is also my impression that this highly specialised activity should involve the identification of missing persons, particularly when it comes to DNA analysis. How come identifications are within the purview of the administration and autopsies are not?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, autopsies are within the purview of the administration, because the administration carries out a series of activities that concern the identification of mortal remains. It organises or rather it organised the collection of ante-mortem information. It organised collection of post-mortem information. It collects operative information about the possible identity of those persons. It collects referential samples for DNA analysis. The administration also carries out preliminary identification of mortal remains. The administration also organises the final identification of mortal remains. It maintains records of all the identified persons, and finally it collects and merges all the documents concerning all the identifications. Autopsies are therefore an integral part of forensic processing of mortal remains, and that documentation is also stored by the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons. I apologise. When it comes to the final identification of mortal remains, an activity that is co-ordinated and organised by the administration for detainees, and missing persons is something that is carried out by competent scientific and medical institutions in co-operation with the victims' families.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just clarify this part of your answer where you said that the administration carries out preliminary identifications. What is that supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means the following: Regarding all missing persons, the administration has in its position ante-mortem data, data concerning the life of the person. After the processing of mortal remains, the mortal remains are delivered to the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons. The administration compares ante-mortem data with post-mortem data and compares them with the circumstances of the finding of the mortal remains and other operative information, and in that way it narrows down a short list of persons to whom these mortal remains could belong. This information is then delivered to the competent scientific and medical persons for them to determine how well founded or not these assumptions are. After that, families are invited for identification with a proviso that, as I wrote in my report, currently all mortal remains are subjected to DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to somehow establish the scope of your examination. In view of your training as described in your CV, to what extent are you able to answer individual questions concerning autopsies, DNA analysis, exhumations, et cetera? In other words, I listened yesterday to your testimony wherein you gave us collective information about all these things and described what is written in those findings. That's something we can see for ourselves. But I'm interested, for instance, are you able to answer questions that concern a specific autopsy report? Why, for instance, the conclusion is what it is about the cause of death, let's say, the time of death, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding questions concerning autopsy reports and their findings, I cannot answer them. I can answer questions concerning organisational aspects, the methodology of the work of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, and the results of our work. As for medical findings, this is a very technical job that is within the competence of forensic medics, and I believe you had an expert witness here who testified about this and that was Professor Davor Strinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but he told us that he could only answer questions concerning autopsy reports that he did himself, not reports made by others. But I understand your answer, and it's all perfectly clear. Would you just tell me, does the same apply to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I don't recall at this stage Dr. Strinovic limiting himself to only reports that he had personally conducted, and I believe if you look at the reports that were admitted through him, there were a number that were conducted by other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I put this question to Dr. Strinovic in my cross-examination, and I cannot say what was part of transcript, but during the break I could identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind to tell me one more thing. Does the same apply to DNA analysis and their findings; for instance, why a person has been identified in precisely that way based on the material that was gathered, or would you be also unable to answer questions about DNA?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can't answer questions about that part of the work. I can only speak about organisational aspects and results.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you attended a certain number of exhumations on the ground, and I wanted to ask did you have an active role on those sites where exhumations were conducted, or were you just an observer?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons organises exhumations and co-ordinates the participants in the process, of course, I, as an officer of this administration, played an active part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just describe that role that you had? I'm talking about the work on exhumation sites.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about communication with other participants in the process of exhumations, with representatives of international organisation, as well as representatives of the competent bodies in charge of searching for missing persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbia who in some cases also attended the exhumations. Furthermore, my role also involved sometimes collecting additional information from families of people suspected of being in the graves, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did family members of the potential victims attend the exhumations themselves?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, no, except at one stage where identifications of mortal remains were carried out on exhumation sites themselves or when personal items were displayed on site for purposes of identification. That was the case of Vukovar, the new cemetery, and Bacin Skela where some mortal remains were identified on site. Then in a certain number of cases of those found in Brkus [phoen], Sarvis Dol [phoen], and Bilje, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the new cemetery at Vukovar. You said, if I'm not mistaken, yesterday that that was a secondary grave, that some mortal remains from Velepromet were reburied there. They were reburied at the new cemetery in Vukovar in December.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar, the new cemetery, is a very particular grave. In a way it can be treated as a secondary grave because that's where mortal remains from Velepromet were transferred there in 19 cases, Trpinjska Cesta 11 cases, Galisov Dol [phoen] 28 cases, Petrovacki Atar, 36 cases. However, in addition to those mortal remains transferred for primary graves, there were also mortal remains in the Vukovar new cemetery of people found in the streets of Vukovar, found in the area of Bogdanovci, a total of 938.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday -- you listed, rather, the organisations with whom your administration co-operates for the purpose of determining whether the missing persons on your list are still missing. That's page 3756 of the transcript. And I noted that in listing all these organisations you did not mention courts. Does it mean you have no such communication with courts in Croatia, of course?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have communication with courts in Croatia and we have very close co-operation with courts considering that all exhumations of mortal remains that are carried out are carried out pursuant to a court order. However, in the part of the work that concerns checking and cross-checking records, I must admit that we did not take advantage of this mechanism, and I'm not really sure how useful that mechanism would be in determining whether a person is possibly alive or not when we have at our disposal other mechanisms and other sources of information that are up-to-date and of very high quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had occasion to take a look at certain Croatian regulations that concern declaring missing persons dead, and I see that it is within the jurisdiction of courts. I'll show you one decision that proves that, which is 1D273 from our list. You will see it on the screen presently. It concerns a person. It doesn't have to be broadcast. I'm not sure to what extent this needs to be public. We will see the translation presently as well. You see, this is a ruling of the Municipal Court in Vukovar declaring or establishing that a certain person is dead. The ruling also establishes the date of death, and we see from this that it is the court in Vukovar that has jurisdiction over establishing somebody's death and the date of their death. That's why I wanted to ask you, do you know out of all those persons that the administration found to be dead, how many have been actually declared dead by a court ruling?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know how many of them have been declared dead by a court decision, but it is a fact that some have been declared dead for the purposes of allowing families to exercise their rights. The families, for instance, are unable to treat issues of marital status or issues of inheritance as long as a person is on record as missing. That's why in some cases families instituted proceedings before a court to have a person declared dead. This document illustrates this very well. This concerns a certain Niko Soljic who was declared dead by a court ruling so that the family can exercise some of its rights, but the fact is that we took over the mortal remains of Niko Soljic from Sremska Mitrovica in 1999 or year 2000, considerably after he was declared dead by a court decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I'm not specifically interested in that -- this person, and we don't have to go into so much detail. I just wanted to illustrate by showing this document that it is the courts, actually, that declare a certain person dead, and as you say, it's for the purpose of allowing families to exercise their rights to benefits and other rights. And I believe that for these purposes, it matters only -- not only that the person is dead but also to establish the date of death as is the case here. So I'd like to know whether and how your commission or administration established the date of death.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration didn't establish the date of death. The date of death is indicated in the declaration or certificate of death issued by the competent scientific medical institution. In a case such as this where we have court proceedings involved, it is the court that determines the date of death. And if you allow me to comment on this case, this case proves exactly what I've been saying. In some cases, although it is not in dispute that persons were missing, families had them declared dead in order to be able to exercise certain rights, and they did so before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood yesterday that all persons who were missing and who were declared dead, at least I believe that was your evidence, and you will correct me if I am wrong, I believe you said all of them had certain rights, all those persons who went missing in the armed conflict and were later found to be dead, except there was a distinction between defenders and civilians in terms of rights. So I concluded that all the people who applied before a court to have a family member declared dead also had a vested interest in having them declared dead, regardless of the fact that somebody was a defender and somebody was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases what was at issue was inheritance, and that does not depend on the status of the person because both families of civilians and families of defenders have the same rights as far as inheritance is concerned. So the families are not interested in having somebody declared dead in terms of status. It usually concerns an issue of marital status or inheritance. For instance, the spouse of a missing person cannot remarry until her husband is declared dead; that is to say, until the moment he has been found and identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, are you saying that one can exercise those rights, that family members can exercise their rights irrespective of the status of the missing persons, be it civilian or a defendant and that it don't have to be based on a court ruling?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't understand your question. I'm not sure that I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat. Does this mean that the families of missing persons could exercise their rights even without a court ruling that that missing person died?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the matters of inheritance or marital status?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't mean inheritance matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the counsel be advised not to overlap because we won't be able to interpret. Could the witness start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam Bilic, you are -- you and Mr. Zivanovic are overlapping and that causes a problem for the interpreters. Could you start again your answer to Mr. Zivanovic's last question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We're talking about the following: According to the laws which are in effect in the Republic of Croatia, including the law on the rights of homeland war veterans and the law on the rights of military and civilian invalids of war, which deals with the status rights of civilians, prescribe certain rights which may be exercised by the families of those persons which are considered missing. A special category are the rights of those persons who have been declared dead or killed. Within their scope, the rights of the families of the missing persons are almost identical to the rights of those who have been declared dead or killed. This means that from the aspect of the rights that arise from the death of their families, the families are not motivated to have the missing persons declared dead, if not from the aspect of those rights that I previously mentioned, and those are the inheritance rights and marital matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, yesterday you spoke about the questionnaire, and you said that you participated in its drafting -- or, rather, in its design, and that you also participated in the training of the personnel that collected information about the missing persons. That is on page 3755 of yesterday's transcript. Could you please tell us whether those questionnaires were filled out by family members personally, those who were looking for their members of family, or were those questionnaires filled out by those persons who had been trained to collect information?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information was collected by the trained personnel of the Red Cross. It was within their job description to possess knowledge, know-how and experience in communicating with the families of the missing persons. The questionnaires we filled out based on the information which was provided to them by people searching for their family members. Every questionnaire had to be signed by the family to confirm the accuracy of the information contained therein. Questionnaires were also signed by the officials of the Croatian Red Cross that filled out those questionnaires.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This means that the questionnaires were filled out by people who were trained to fill them out.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to have undergone training.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you participated in that training?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On line 1 -- could you please look at P2324, a Prosecution exhibit. While we are waiting for the document to appear, as far as I could understand you, yesterday you stated that the administration searched for all the citizens of Croatia who had gone missing in armed conflict irrespective of their ethnic background or religious affiliation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that the two pages done not correspond to each other, i.e., the translation that we see on the screen does not correspond to the B/C/S original. Could we perhaps go to the following page, maybe that will help, or perhaps even one page further. Let's go to the following page quickly. Now we have both versions. Could you please tell me, when it comes to this questionnaire, how come -- what was the reason why ethnic background was included in it? How would such information be of help in searching for a living person and especially of a dead person?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you yesterday, information on ethnic background was considered general information. This is customary information normally used in questionnaires. It is even used by the International Committee of the Red Cross. I apologise. When we're talking about the design of the questionnaire, you will find it in my report, and I testified to that effect yesterday, that in designing it we used the questionnaire produced by the United Nations Centre for Human Rights, the search centre, and the ICRC questionnaire. That questionnaire which was our starting point in designing our own questionnaire also contains information about ethnic background, the ethnic background of the missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, in was taken over from the form used by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst other institutions that use such questionnaires. The ICRC is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about item 14? Was that also taken over from that same questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why then was that included in this form, because I don't see how this can help in searching for a missing person or somebody's mortal remains?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. I agree with you, but at that moment it was included. I really can't remember what were the underlying motives 20 years ago to have it included, but I agree with you that it really cannot help the search process. The only thing I can say is that I absolutely do not remember any case where religion was used. It was never analysed. It was never used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that this information was never used or analysed, do you mean that the administration has never used it or analysed it, or do you have in mind some other bodies?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that in general terms this was not done. The missing person dossiers are stored in the files of the Administration of Detainees and Missing Persons, and this is the only institution that these files are available, accessible to -- anybody else who wants to get hold of the information has to file a request to the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons and explain the reasons for which the information from those files will be used. I guarantee you that the information on religious affiliations have never been used or analysed by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now go to the following page. Please look at item 18, the questionnaire entry number 18. Question 18 concerns the affiliation of the missing persons to an armed formation. There's a list of seven -- seven armed formations listed under (a) through (g). What I would like to know is this: How were your staff trained to be able to identify whether the missing person in question belonged to one of the seven formations that are listed in here?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information on the status of missing persons were collected by the ICRC members based on the information provided by the victim's family. In other words, the source of such information were the missing persons' families.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, within the framework of the examiners' training, were they told how to differentiate between the seven military formations?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They relied on the families statements. Our staff were not educated about that. The only logical thing was to instruct them to encircle the answer provided to them by the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at chapter 2 on the same page. Let's look at item 8. That's question 8. It concerns forcible abduction and who did it, and on the following page you see all the options. I believe that there is a total of six possible options or ways to answer that question. Or even more, perhaps even seven or eight. How, if at all, were people who collected data educated and trained? How did they instruct the families as to how to identify, how to distinguish between these categories? For example, a JNA member, on the one hand, and a member of the Territorial Defence of the JNA on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like in the case of the previous question, the source of such information were families and the information that they were privy to. The officials of the Red Cross staff did not instruct families how to distinguish between those people who may have participated in the abduction. What we envisage here is the most predictable answers. The information on who was responsible for the disappearance or a forcible abduction was provided by the families based on the information that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, in some cases when you look at these questionnaires, you see that family members even pointed to some very specific persons who abducted their family members. In many other situations they simply said paramilitaries, civilians, or something along those lines. What I would like to know is whether trainers were expected to explain the difference to help them answer this question; for example, could they be more specific and say that their family member was abducted by a person wearing partly military, partly civilian uniform?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both families and ICRC staff could opt out from this question if they couldn't answer it. If they knew, when they knew, who was responsible for forcible abduction, in those cases they could provide an answer. Like you said it yourself, in those questionnaires that you inspected, very often you have seen that the information does not have that information, that they don't know the persons who carried out the forcible abduction, and they leave out question number 2 where it says say what you know about the aforementioned persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you worded those questions, what was expected under the suggestion that one's family member was taken away by a member of secret services? How could they have known that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There are various options. Many possibilities are given. I don't even remember a single answer where that was encircled. However, we try to envisage a variety of possibilities in order to facilitate choices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on these questionnaires, those that were filled out, did the administration carry out any checks of the data thus received from those who were looking for their family members?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what regard or in what part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Any.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very broad question. Of course the administration carried out checks on different occasions regarding the list of missing persons itself which was being created based on these questionnaires. Next, checks were carried out in terms of family members pertaining to the part which refers to family and educational status. Information was collected and kept up-to-date as regards their residence, which was also necessary in order to take their blood samples and to organise the final stage of identification. Furthermore, checks were also carried out to obtain medical documentation in the medical institutions where the families had mentioned the medical records of those missing could be found. So certain checks were done that could have a specific impact on resolving the cases of missing persons. They have been carried out, and they still are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have any information about those checks, or at least for many of the people, I'll address that topic separately. Now, tell me this, please: What was the date that was taken as the date of disappearance if it was used as the date of death?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you already that we did not determine nor do we determine the date of death. It comes from the report on the fact of death issued by the competent medical institution and court decision. As regards the date of disappearance, perhaps if we can go one page back in the questionnaire and then I can tell you precisely what number it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we go one page back, please, then.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the date of disappearance, we relied on the piece of information stated in question number 1 in the second set of information, that is to say information on abduction, disappearance, or capture of the person sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In a number cases I could observe that that information differed from the information collected on when the person was last seen alive. I think -- well, I don't know what page this is, but I think it was on the page after that.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on page 4 or 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is in the B/C/S text. I think in the English it is on page 5. Yes. Item 21.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think another question from the previous page also refers to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That may well be. Let's see. No. It's probably page 4 in English?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless, I can try to answer. It has to do with the fact that the questionnaire was drafted in late 1993, and information was gathered in early 1994, which is over two years after most of these people disappeared -- or, rather, most of the forcible removals had taken place at that time. Having in mind that the families in the meantime undertook certain measures themselves, talking to different witnesses, and given the fact that they obtained certain information, we envisaged an entire set of questions pertaining to when the missing person was last seen alive. The families cited all information they had available, for the most part not citing the reliability of their sources. In most cases, such information, unfortunately, were not useful in the process of tracing, such as information when people tried to find their family members by showing the photographs of their missing family members, and then people will tell them, "Yes, I saw him there at that time." In a small number of cases such information did indeed prove to be true, but we could only establish that once the case file was actually closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you mentioned some specific cases; inter alia, you said that only recently the identity of Haso Brajic has been established, whose mortal remains were allegedly found in Celije.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why it took 15 years to establish this person's identity?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to. The person in question resided in the Republic of Croatia, in Osijek. Haso Brajic was married, but he and his wife did not have children. By -- well, Haso Brajic hailed from Bosnia. His relatives, that is to say sisters and family members, that we had no information whatsoever at the time, moved elsewhere during the war. The mortal remains were treated by DNA method, but we did not have reference samples. Thus we had nothing to compare the mortal remains to. We asked for assistance of the competent bodies in Bosnia-Herzegovina in ascertaining the places of residence of his relatives and kin. The moment we received such information, we asked for the assistance of the International Commission for Missing Persons, who is otherwise our partner in the process of identification. They took blood samples from the found family members. By virtue of comparing them to the mortal remains, it was established that there was a match. It was established that the mortal remains found in Celije were those of Haso Brajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the time of his death, was it ascertained by the administration?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration did not deal with that. It only had the date of his disappearance at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit 1964 from the Prosecution list. It is the questionnaire for Haso Brajic. Can we look at page 10 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S version. Sorry, I don't think it is the page. Perhaps it is page 18 in B/C/S. No. No. Page 10. Sorry. We need to go back to the page that was on the screen a moment ago. That's the right beige in the B/C/S version. I'm just verifying the page in the English. I think it's the next page in English. Yes. That's it. We have it all. If you look at under (c), was the person sought ever treated in a medical institution. You can see there that Haso Brajic was treated in the general hospital in Osijek in 1992 and 1993. At the pulmonary department in Osijek also in 1992 and 1993. On the other hand, we have information that he went missing in 1991, in September. That kind of data raises doubts as to his identification, in my view. I wanted to ask you this: Given the fact that we do not have any official information on his identification and we cannot explain how that person ended up in Celije allegedly in that mass grave, although he seemed to have been in Osijek in 1992 and 1993, does the administration, given its policy of keeping that material, those documents, allow for any checks to be carried out in cases of identifications such as this one?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. First of all, I'd like to ask if we could go back to page 2 in this questionnaire for Haso Brajic. Yes. The date of disappearance, it is stated unknown. Can we go to page 8. I just wanted to make sure whether his family or his wife ever mentioned any dates. Sorry, not page 8. Page 4, where we have information on when the person was seen for the last time. Yes. If we look at number 29: Are there any circumstances indicating that the missing person was killed or perished? And it is stated "yes." A newspaper article dated the 22nd of April, 1992, from the "Glas Slavonije" newspaper is cited. From this I conclude that his wife, when providing information on his treatment in Osijek in the hospital, she probably simply made a mistake. I apologise. That's what my conclusion is, because if we here have an article published on April 22, 1992, and it indicates that Haso Brajic may have been killed or perished, then it can only logically be concluded that there was a simple mistake when information was provided as to his treatment in the hospital. He couldn't have been treated in the hospital in 1993 if in 1992 his wife stated that there was information indicating that he had been killed. As regards any additional possibilities to verify findings, this case was identified through a joint project between the International Commission for Missing Persons and the Administration for the Detainees and Missing Persons. It is not an identification process undertaken by the Republic of Croatia independently and alone. It was carried out through a joint project with a renowned international organisation, and their data is credibly relied on whenever DNA analysis is discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something about this newspaper article given the fact that you are an expert and that you work for the administration. What weight does the administration and you as expert attach to a newspaper piece? Judging by your answer, one would conclude that you accept it as absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a question of whether I accept or whether we accept newspaper articles as something that is absolutely true. What I'm saying is this: If the family stated that according to a newspaper article from 1992 there is indicia that Haso Brajic had been killed, then that runs completely against the information they provided on his treatment in 1992 and 1993. If he had been treated in the Osijek hospital in 1993, his wife would not have stated that in 1992 he was probably dead. So we are discussing facts here rather than assigning weight to a newspaper article. The sequence of events is the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You yourself say that there is indicia pertaining to that newspaper article, and that was the thrust of my question. What weight would you assign to a newspaper article published during the war on the other side of the front line; that is to say, not by people who may have been eyewitnesses. You also say that the only logical conclusion is that the data on his health status is inaccurate in terms of the dates of treatment. What I'm trying to point out is that I think that another conclusion is possible, and that is that the information contained in the article is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that some of the information is inaccurate. I don't know. I can't see this newspaper article. But we are talking now about time, about years. If he had been treated in the Osijek hospital in 1993, then his wife would not have stated that he was possibly dead since 1992. This issue is about the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say? He was dead in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's question -- or, rather, the answer, the -- 29, namely: "Are there any circumstances indicating that the missing person was killed?" And the answer is: "Yes. The newspaper article from 22 April, 1992, 'Glas Slavonije.'" So the newspaper article contains that information, and the reference to this treatment here is in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just one moment. Ms. Bilic, the information about the newspaper article, if I understand you correctly, is given by the man's wife; is that right? That's an answer to the question put to her; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the information about treatment in the hospital --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's on. Just one moment. Is it okay now? Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The information about the treatment in the hospital in 1993 is also given by the wife in response to a question. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So what you're saying is it wouldn't be logical for her to say on the one hand there is information that he was killed in 1992, and on the other hand give the information that he was treated in 1993 in a hospital. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. And from that I conclude that it must be a confusion, a mistake, and this is additionally supported by the fact of the identification of the mortal remains of Haso Brajic, which is consistent with the answer provided by his wife to question 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to the last page to see the date when the wife of Haso Brajic provided this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose this is the newspaper story that you relied on, but that's not what I wanted to show you. I wanted to show you this date. Can you see it? Although it's rather pale, but I believe the year is 1994. At least we can see the year.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is year 1994, and that was the first drive for collecting information on missing person. I would just like to correct one thing. We did not rely on the newspaper story. The information from the newspaper story was provided by Haso Brajic's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The date is 8 February 1994. Now, you just said that this identification was done by the ICMP, the commission for missing persons from Bosnia-Hercegovina, or was it Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters of the ICMP is in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I said this identification was done in cooperation between the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons and the International Commission for Missing Persons in a concluded project which was called Joint Project for Final DNA Identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to know something else. Did you -- or, rather, did the commission get from the other commission only the finding or did it get the finding complete, all the supporting information including electropherograms?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration received from the ICMP the findings of the analyses of blood samples of Haso Brajic's relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the administration get only the final conclusions or the electropherograms underlying the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly did not get the blood samples. We got the findings. Whether those findings are only figures or the electropherograms as well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because it is very well known that the ICMP does not provide this to anyone. In many situations, they were unwilling to provide such things even to this Tribunal, and I don't mean this case, I mean other cases, and I'm asking you this to find out whom we could possibly address, you, your administration, or the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as providing the findings of the analysis of mortal remains including electropherograms, I can tell you that we have ICMP findings. We have findings in those identification cases that were part of a joint project between the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons and the ICMP. Through that joint project the mortal remains of approximately 300 to 350 persons have been identified. The figure may be even higher, and in more than 100 cases it was actually a confirmation of findings that the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons produced already which functions as a control mechanism, but we do take into account all the information that concerns either the processing and analysis of mortal remains and blood samples equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you specifically about electropherograms and you said you don't know. Now you say you exchange with them all data. Now I'd like to know where we stand. Do you receive also electropherograms or not, or electropherograms are not included in this concept of all data that you received from them?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the specific case of Haso Brajic I cannot maintain at this moment that we do have in our possession the electropherograms. It doesn't mean yes or no. It just means I don't know at this moment. Otherwise, I maintain that we exchange with ICMP all findings and all data concerning the joint project of DNA analysis of mortal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in other situations you do have electropherograms?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we do in the majority of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, would this be a good time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I remind you for after the break not to overlap, please. Ms. Bilic, we take the first break, come back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the questionnaire again, that's Exhibit 2324, I would like to look at page 2, item 8. It seems I need page 3, question 8. This is -- this is the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just need the right page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The question 8 is: "Who carried out the forcible taking away/capture of the person?" And then we see listed various armed forces. We could say enemy armed forces from the viewpoint of the Croatian armed forces, and my question would be: What is the reason why no Croatian formations have been listed here. None of the Croatian forces that are also listed in the same questionnaire, more precisely seven of them, if you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did understand your question. The thing is that in most cases, as far as persons whose families initiated tracing requests are concerned, the fact that they went missing is the responsibility of one of these formations. However, under (g) we see "Other," and that leaves the possibility of indicating any other formation, including some formations of the Croatian armed forces if the families had reason to believe that they were responsible for forcibly taking away or capturing their family member. So this list makes it possible to provide any answer based on the information available to the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me the reason why these formations are not expressly indicated as they are indicated in that other paragraph? Why aren't they mentioned by name as they are mentioned on another page?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said before, most of the abductions in cases of forcibly taking people away, the person who had gone missing and reported in that drive in 1994 was the responsibility of the formations listed here, and the possibility is also given of mentioning the Croatian armed formation if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to another passage on a different page, one page before this; that is, information on the membership in some forces of the person sought. You see from item (a) to item (i) various possibilities are listed. Can you explain to me why this does not mention that the said person is possibly a member of the formations we saw listed on the previous page, the Yugoslav Army, Territorial Defence, paramilitaries, secret services, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that this questionnaire on missing persons needs to be viewed in the context in which it came into being. It is a good instrument for collecting information wherein individual questions reflect the situation that prevailed at that moment. There are also -- there were also some questions here that should be reformulated today concerning UNPA zones and refugee status, et cetera. As to your question why members of the JNA and paramilitary formations are concerned or whatever you want to call them, most of the missing persons who went missing in 1991 and 1992 were Croatian defenders or civilians who went missing or were forcibly taken away by JNA and paramilitary forces. Their families addressed the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons and initiated the procedure of the search with the administration. The families of missing members of the JNA addressed and contacted the competent commission for the search for missing persons of the Republic of Serbia, or more precisely at that time it was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whereas members of paramilitary units addressed the commission of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina. The fact is that in previously occupied territories, there was also an established body that dealt with the missing persons who were members of paramilitary formations or captured members of paramilitary formations. The headquarters of that commission was in Knin. However, one of its branches dealt with captured and missing persons in the Croatian part of the Danube valley, and its headquarters was in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that owing to the fact that that commission existed in the territory that was at the time in the hands of the Serbian forces, the administration didn't initiate any more serious proceedings, as it were, to search for the members of those formations that had gone missing in armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That doesn't mean that. The administration actually did carry out searches, but when it started procedures to collect data on missing persons, an invitation was seen out to the families of those citizens of the Republic of Croatia who had gone missing to report to the administration and to report the disappearance of their members. That invitation was published in the media on the eve of that drive, and it was intended for all those citizens whose family member had gone missing in the Republic of Croatia during the war. The fact is, however, that at the same time, the other commissions were being set up which dealt with the same issue in the previously occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia. For example, those para-authorities' commissions were active, and they appeared as the other side in the negotiations together with us, whereas the families of the disappeared members of the JNA and the TO mostly resided in the then occupied areas of Republic of Croatia and sent their search requests those commissions that were in charge of those issues. That was the situation as it was in 1994 -- or, rather, in 1993 and 1994 when our questionnaires were designed and when information was collected. Later on, and especially today, the situation has changed dramatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's stick to the questionnaire. I don't want to talk about the situation as it is today. I apologise for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem at all. What I'm trying to say is that this questionnaire reflects the context within which it was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And for that reason, if I understand you properly, this question 18 does not actually comprise members of various formations or, rather, armed formations that are listed under 8 on the following page, i.e., members of the JNA, the police, the Territorial Defence, paramilitary formations, secret services, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one -- just one moment. We are overlapping again, and, Mr. Zivanovic, as far as this is a question, isn't that asked and answered extensively?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at 3747 which is another questionnaire and it concerns somebody called Vinko Oroz. In English I'm interested in page 14. The corresponding page in B/C/S is 10. There seems to be a mistake. Anyway, let's look at chapter 2, question number 10. I believe that this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4 in B/C/S. I apologise. And I believe that it should be on the last page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the entry under number 10. It says here, and it is the last sentence: "The person who submitted the application has learned --" I apologise. It's not what I wanted to read. It's a mistake. We will drop this exhibit. I have to withdraw this document. I made a mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3765 is the next document I would like to look at. Page 5. I apologise. It's page 4, and the question number is 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that this person was last seen in late February 1992 in Darda, in the police station there. He was recorded as somebody who was killed on the 4th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, what I have on the screen in English is "date and hour," number 21: "Date and hour when the missing person was last seen, end of November 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have in the B/C/S it is the end of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see whether we can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. It appears --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 21. 21. Yeah. That's the one. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you make any checks of these allegations, i.e., that he was last seen in February 1992 at the police station in Darda?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember as I sit here. I can't remember whether any checks were carried out in this specific case, especially not in terms of his last sighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This question concerns this person, so if you do not remember anything them, let's leave it at that. If you don't have a precise answer to my question, let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me whether there were any additional checks carried out, I can say that I can't remember. However, when it comes to this person, specifically I know that his post-mortem remains were located and identified. As far as I remember, they were found in the Republic of Serbia and taken over from there. I believe that we have at our disposal documentation showing the time when those mortal remains were taken out from the Danube River.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The RCMP carried out the identification?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case it was done by a DNA laboratory in the Republic of Croatia. I would like to add the following: His mortal remains were buried, if I remember it well, in Novi Sad, and then in 2002 pursuant to an agreement with the commission and Republic of Serbia, we organised the taking of samples from non-identified mortal remains buried in Novi Sad. One of the samples that were taken were subsequent -- subsequently identified as belonging to this particular person, and then by applying the DNA method, his identity was established, and then the mortal remains were taken over. Before we had a positive ID, we did not know what had happened to that person, and we didn't know where his mortal remains were buried. The control sample of non-identified persons from Novi Sad can be found with the ICMP. However, these findings were arrived at independently by my administration. I apologise. I hope that we are talking about the exact person. There are two persons by the name of Siles, Janes in Tibor. Could we possibly go back -- or, rather, I have the materials in front of me. With your leave, I would like to peruse the materials that I have in front of me just to make sure that I'm not confused about the identity of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my time is limited. I just wanted to know whether the administration checked these allegations. That is all. You have given me a satisfactory answer when you said that you cannot be very precise in terms of my question, so we will not go on analysing this document. Let's now look at 31 -- 3931, which is another exhibit from the Prosecutor's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in page 4 in B/C/S and page 5 in English. Question number 20. Can we go one page back. Here at the bottom of the page -- I apologise. Can we go back to the page that we had on the screen just a while ago. We had it on the screen and then we went one page back. Can you forward one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the answer under 20, the last answer on this page. It says here: "His mother alleges that he was seen in Sremska Mitrovica." This person, as far as I know -- or, rather, I would like to ask you the same. Did you ever check whether that person was indeed in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all the missing persons we checked whether they were in the territory either in the Republic of Serbia or Bosnia-Herzegovina depending on the case. A list of all the missing persons was submitted to the competent bodies of the Republic of Serbia, especially of those persons for which we had information that they may be detained in the Republic of Serbia. As far as we know, we did not get a confirmation that that person was in Sremska Mitrovica. The only mechanism available to us for checking this kind of information were negotiations, i.e., bilateral relations with the corresponding commission of the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at 4063, please. The name is Ivan Redzic. We can move to page 3 and then to page 4 in B/C/S, and pages 4 then 5 in English. Do you see here at the very bottom - again we should look at question 20 - it is said that this person, on the 4th of December, 1992, was seen at the Vukovar Hospital by an interpreter working for UNPROFOR. The interpreter's name is indicated, and that he had surgery on his arm at the hospital. When he was supposed to be taken over, he left the hospital, and in May 1993 he was seen in Borovo Naselje under a different name?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the answer to this is contained in my previous explanation when I said that one set of questions focuses on when the missing person was last seen, because we proceeded from the assumption that -- we proceeded from the knowledge and the assumption that in that interval, in the two and a half years, families have found something out, and here in this case we also have a witness who was apparently together with the detainees in Dalj, but in many cases this information proved to be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand your answer's a general one and you've already provided it before, but I'm interested in this specific situation: Did you check with the interpreter of the UNPROFOR identified here? Did she indeed see Ivan Redzic as we can read here?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday about a French national who went missing, Jean Michel Nicolier, and you said that he has the status of Croatian defender, and that as far as you know this status necessarily requires Croatian citizenship. I'd like to know do you know for sure that he has the status of Croatian defender? Is this verified information?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, subsequently, and I mean a couple of years ago, he was granted the status of Croatian defender, but this part is not within my purview. That is not the kind of information in my questionnaire. So what I'm saying now is what I know from the media. His family visited Croatia several times, including in order to provide blood samples for DNA analysis, and as far as I remember, he was granted the status of Croatian defender and included in the register of Croatian defenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Croatian citizenship is a requirement for that status. Is that reliable information?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not reliable information. I said as far as I know I believe that is so, but I'm not so familiar with regulations as to be able to speak of this in any qualified way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Milorad Stricevic yesterday and his identification.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said his family never made a tracing request in Croatia or in Serbia or before the ICRC. That's on page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the page number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how was the identification performed on Milorad Stricevic?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By DNA analysis. The family was given the findings of DNA analysis and also the findings of analysis by traditional methods, but we had operative information as well indicating that among the mortal remains from Daljski Atar there were also the mortal remains of Milorad Stricevic. We found his relatives, including his brother. We took blood samples from his brother, and based on that we established his identity by DNA analysis, and those results coincided with the results of traditional analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Giving evidence on this matter, you also said that year 1998 could not possibly be the year of his death, although it is indicated as such. Can you tell me why is it impossible?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established that the mortal remains belonging to Milorad Stricevic were found and extracted from the well in Daljski Atar. As I said yesterday, the mortal remains from Daljski Atar belonged to the locals of Erdut who were taken on several occasions away from their homes. Closer to the bottom of the well were mortal remains of those who were taken away first and thrown into the well, and then as they were taken away in groups one after another, they were thrown into the well group by group, so the topmost group of mortal remains was the group taken away the last. I do not have here information here about Milorad Stricevic, but by the location of his remains in that well, it is possible to approximately establish at what time his mortal remains were thrown into the well, but they were certainly nowhere near the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: His mortal remains are designated as 1387.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me the acronym next to the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at this moment. But are you saying that you are not sure whether his mortal remains were at the bottom or in the middle or the top?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without this specific designation in front of me, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then how did you establish that he was not thrown into the well in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that can be established, among other things, from the condition of the mortal remains. The exhumation was in 1998, and if he had been killed near 1998, then his mortal remains would have been better preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And to what extent were they preserved?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but that can be established by looking into the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if the cause of his death was established?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. That's a question for forensic medical experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One last thing I would like to ask you. You said that the exhumation started at Ovcara in September 1996. Could you tell us which authorities were in government in that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time within the process of peaceful reintegration the UNTS force was present in the Croatian Danube valley area and the Croatian authorities did not have full control of that territory. Did not have full sovereignty there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any Serbian authorities at that time in that place during the peaceful reintegration?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but I do not know what their mandate was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Hadzic was the head of that government, that local government?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In line 25, page 42 -- or, rather, line 24, the acronym is not UNST. It is UNTAES.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gillett, redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes, there's a couple of matters to clear up, thanks. I was going to say at the outset that my colleague said he would get back to us after the break with a reference to where Dr. Strinovic limited himself in terms of the autopsies he could comment on, so if you're able to provide that at some point that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Bilic, turning to some of the issues that were raised in cross-examination. Firstly you were asked about the questionnaire for Haso Brajic, and this is 65 ter document 1964. In that document, in the section about his medical history, the Defence has raised this reference to treatment in 1992 and 1993 at the Osijek general hospital. Could we please get 65 ter document 1964 on the monitor, please. And if we could go to page 16 of the English and page 14 of the B/C/S. Now, these medical documents were attached to the missing persons questionnaire. Can I ask firstly is it typical that there -- or were there sometimes medical documents attached like this to missing persons questionnaires?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly typical if the family had any medical documentation. Moreover, with every questionnaire, and that was also stressed in the letter of invitation, the families were asked to provide all documentation that they have, including medical records, and attach it to the questionnaire, which in this case was done. There are cases where we have the medical documentation and it forms an integral part of the missing persons file.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: This document refers to the patient Haso Brajic being treated for diabetes at Osijek General Hospital. So what would this suggest about the reference earlier in the form to the treatment in 1992 or 1993? I'm sorry, I should say this appears to be from the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The date indicated here is 1981, and I believe it's the same disease, diabetes. The difference is that the questionnaire indicates a different period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And now if we go to page 4 of the English and B/C/S of the same document, question 22. This lists the address when the individual was last seen before he disappeared, and the address is Oraski Put near Erdut. Now, if in fact he had last been seen at the Osijek General Hospital, wouldn't that be listed as the address where he was last seen?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very probably. Very probably. In that case the location of last sighting would have been indicated as the Osijek hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get document 3747 on the monitor, please, and this is the missing persons questionnaire relating to Janos Siles. Now, in relation to this individual, a mention of the sighting in 1992 was highlighted, I believe. If we could get document 1D264, and that was on the Defence list, and at page 1 of 1D264. And I recall that you said in this case with this individual, you remembered that his remains were taken over from the Republic of Serbia. If we look at 1D264, and it should be entry number 3, we see a markation after his date of birth, N.S. 1086/91. Do you know what that indicates?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a designation of mortal remains, and there's also an indication of the year when they were found. This year when they were found was established based on the documentation that the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons received during negotiations from the competent authorities of the Republic of Serbia.
