That is the time when the mortal remains were extracted from the Danube River, after which they were autopsied and buried at the Novi Sad cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what is the date in this case for Janos Siles, the year?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year when the mortal remains were found -- oh, sorry. 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLET
utterances.text: If we could now get P1507 on the monitor, and this was a document that was admitted yesterday, and this relates to Ivan Redzic, whose state was raised at transcript page 39 of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, I note on the document referred to during cross-examination, the date of disappearance for Ivan Redzic is listed as 19 November 1991. If we look at P1507, which is the list of remains exhumed from Dalj Catholic cemetery, we also see 19 November 1991. My question is: When these bodies were exhumed, and you indicated yesterday you were involved in the exhumation, how were the bodies arranged? Were they in a group? If we could scroll down to the bottom of the page in B/C/S. We should see him at entry number 4.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mortal remains were in a group. It is a classical mass grave found at the Catholic cemetery in Dalj. The mortal remains were found at a considerable depth, and above the victims from this mass grave were buried persons who had died in the meantime, possibly even of natural causes. In any case, above these mortal remains there were other bodies buried, which made the exhumation considerably more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, those were all the issues I had for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I would just give the reference for Dr. Strinovic part of evidence. It is transcript pages 2390 through 2393, 8 January, 8 January 2013.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. There may have been some confusion. When we looked at those pages, it appeared Strinovic was talking about exhumations. In fact, one specific exhumation report that he said he wasn't involved in drafting and -- and was not talking about autopsy reports conducted by other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, this brings an end to your testimony. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Biersay. Is the next witness available?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe -- I believe he is, Your Honour. If that's the Court's preference, to go straight into it and then take the break, I'm happy to oblige.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The next witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Trial Chamber. First of all, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us your first and family name, your date of birth, and your nationality and/or ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hicham Malla. I was born in 1943 in Damask. I'm currently a citizen of Croatia, and I am of Syrian ethnic background. I was born in Damascus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you that by doing so you'll expose yourself to the penalty of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful information to this Tribunal. Can I ask you to read now the solemn declaration the usher will hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Malla.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described to the Trial Chamber that you are currently a citizen of Croatia. Could you tell the Trial Chamber for how long you have lived in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Since 1964.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you complete your university studies?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what did you study?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what was your profession after you completed those studies?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I became a general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Trial Chamber how it came to be that you studied in Zagreb and stayed afterwards?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: When I graduated, I got married. I found a job in Zagreb, and I stayed in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the nationality or ethnicity of your wife?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you have children?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I have a daughter and a son. Two children, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you live in Croatia in 1990 through 1991?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: In Borovo Naselje in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you working in 1991, at the beginning of 1991?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: At the beginning of the year I was in Zagreb. I was a resident in occupational medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard about Borovo Naselje. Briefly, could you describe where Borovo Naselje is in relation to Borovo or Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Borovo Naselje is a neighbourhood which was built for the staff of Borovo, whereas Borovo Selo is an old village which is about 2 or 3 kilometres away from the new settlement known as Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the company named Borovo?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. It was a huge company which had a lot of different production segments, rubber production, shoe production. It even had its construction part. Borovo also had its own medical centre known as the Borovo Medical Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you ever work for that company, the Borovo company?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes, from 1982 when I joined as a GP.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many other doctors, if any, worked at Borovo?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: In 1982 there were eight of us, and gradually the number grew to 80.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you able to approximate the number of employees that worked for the Borovo company?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: There were between 21- to 23.000 people working in Borovo, and there are about 3.000 people on top of that working all over Croatia in the Borovo shops and stores.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described that you were doing a residency in occupational medicine. Were you working sometimes at the Borovo company in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever necessary, when another colleague was on sick leave or on holiday, I would come to help out, make up the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In addition to being a doctor with the Borovo company, did you work in any other capacity?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. I was a sports physician or a -- the football club physician. There was also a boxing club that I was in charge of, the handball club Borovo, as well as the Borovo karate club. Those were all clubs and teams which were sponsored by the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What local clubs were you the physician for?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The club's name was Sindzelic from Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you become the physician for the Trpinja football club?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The president of that club in 1982 was Mr. Dokmanovic. He got in touch with me. He told me that they needed a doctor part time. I accepted the offer, and I continued working for the club.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What is Mr. Dokmanovic's first name, if you remember? Well, let me ask you this: When you were working as a physician for the Trpinja football club, what was the nature of your contact or relationship with Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I served as the club's physician, and he was the president of the club. We saw each other every week at games, and we socialised after games, and then on Monday I would examine the players for injuries or for possible treatments that had to be administered.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear the answer of the witness on the first question what is Mr. Dokmanovic's first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. -- the witness gave an answer, but I may be wrong. Did you answer that question, Mr. Malla, what Mr. Dokmanovic's first name is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not answer, but the name escapes me. I can give you the name of his brother, but his name, no. The brain's gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What is the name of his brother?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Jovan.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did his brother work?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: In the central warehouse of the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did any other family member of Mr. Dokmanovic work at the Borovo company?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: His wife also worked in the central warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What contacts, if any, would you have with either the -- Mr. Dokmanovic's wife or brother?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: We saw each other often, because we would often go to Dokmanovic's home. My wife and myself went there for celebrations for -- for example, when we had the football club celebrations his wife would attend. My wife would attend as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How would Mr. Dokmanovic usually dress when you knew him back then?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Always in a suit, sporting a tie. He was an engineer. He was a gentleman. He was also a politician, and he always wore suits. Now I've remembered his name. Slavko was his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And Dr. Malla, when you refer to going to the house of Dr. -- of Mr. Dokmanovic, which Dokmanovic are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you describe the clothing worn by Mr. Dokmanovic, which Dokmanovic are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Engineer Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to move towards the middle of 1991. Did there come a time when you sent your children to live somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. When the school ended in the month of July, the Red Cross organised the departure of our children to the coast. My son was ten and a half at the time. I sent him to the coast. And my daughter remained with me for another ten days or so, and then I sent her to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay -- sorry. Ms. Biersay, would you allow me for one moment. Still on Slavko Dokmanovic, Mr. Malla. The time you worked with him or he was the president of the football club and you were working in that football club, did you at that time know his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that whole village was a Serbian village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trpinja was a Serbian village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That is perhaps the next to my next question: How did you know that he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the way he talked and by the village he came from. Everybody knew. I was invited to their religious holidays, to their religious feasts. Those were religious holidays, so everybody knew who they were and what they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I see the time indeed. Thank you. Mr. Malla, this is the time for our second break. Even if you're in only for 15 minutes we have to take the break now. We come back at 12.45. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, are you comfortably seated?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Right before the break we talked about your children, and you described how you sent them out of the area where you live, which was Borovo Naselje. Could you explain why you did that?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Shelling had started around Borovo and around Vukovar. War activities had already started.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe the intensity of that shelling?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: For example, the kindergarten in the centre of Borovo Naselje was shelled, so people were afraid, and they sent children away from Borovo Naselje and Vukovar. Some left in the organisation of the Red Cross and some left individually in the organisation of their own parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the shelling intensified in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. It intensified. The biggest attack was on the 26th of August, early in the morning, around 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you when that happened?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I was at home. My wife, however, left for work in the Borovo company at 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on the 26th of August, 1991, what, if any, structures were shelled?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Most of the neighbourhood and the Borovo company itself. In other words, individual civilian structures and the company, the factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you go to the factory that day of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I couldn't. That's how strong the shelling was. We all had to go down into an atomic shelter. I was very concerned about my wife. I didn't know what was happening with her until that afternoon when she was finally able to come to the company shelter herself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe going into the shelter. Could you describe which shelter that was? The one that you went into.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: In my own building in Borovo Naselje there were three such shelters and a lot of basements. That shelter where I went to could accommodate up to 400 people. It was completely under the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you stay in the shelter for an extended period of time?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Until the fall of Vukovar. That's how long we stayed in the shelter. For three months altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how many people were in shelter with you approximately?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Sometimes it was full to capacity of 400 people, and then their number reduced to 300. They were mostly my neighbours, whole families, children, elderly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What ethnicity or nationality were the people in the shelter, if you know? Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: They were all inhabitants of Borovo Naselje of all ethnicity, Croat, Serb, Ruthenians.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you do for the sick or injured in the Borovo Naselje area?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I did what I could. I couldn't do any surgeries, of course. If somebody had to undergo a major surgery, I would send them to the hospital in Vukovar, and if there was no room in the hospital for recovering patients, they would send them to me if they were just recovering from major procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were these people for whom you were giving care -- where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: In the shelter. There were three atomic shelters which could accommodate up to 1.500 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did the sick and injured stay in the atomic shelter the entire time, or did they move somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: They stayed there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to direct your attention to the 8th of November, 1991. Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: What month is it? When you say November, what month is it? Yes. On the 8th of that month, I was in the atomic shelter. That entire night there was shelling. There was a major attack. And then around 8.00 they called me and said that there were some people wounded in front of the shelter. I took my bag. My wife went with me because I didn't have a nurse. She helped me. We walked from the shelter for some 20 metres, then we saw a car ablaze. There was a man behind the wheel who was already dead. He had been hit. And next to him was a child of some 9 years of age who was wounded. I could see blood coming out of the child's chest, so I took the child out. At that moment a person came out of the shelter who owned a car and took the child to the hospital. After that, the wife whose husband got killed in the car and whose child was taken to the hospital came to see me, but she was in a state of shock, so I gave her some tranquiliser. At that moment a shell fell. I fainted. My wife got killed on the spot, and that patient was wounded, and there were two other people who got wounded. The shell blast threw me for perhaps 5 metres, which I realized only when I came to after I'd fainted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you -- excuse me. When you came to, what injuries had you sustained?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I was covered in blood. I was bleeding from top to bottom. They drove me to Borovo Komerc, which is the Borovo warehouse. A doctor was there, Dr. Emedi. They took me there together with my wife, and the doctor confirmed my wife's death. He treated my wounds. He put stitches on my head, and I had 43 pieces of shrapnel over my body, my back, my legs. My complete body was pierced by the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at our translation, Dr. Malla, and it reads that you had two to three pieces of shrapnel over your body. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I still have them, 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you have two or three or did you have 43 as in 4-3? We're having a problem with our -- with the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Forty-three pieces of shrapnel in my body, most of which were removed in Zagreb, but I still have a few left in my body.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber the -- where the wound was on your head from the shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The injury was here. It was stitched from here to here. I have scars here, the entire back. There are many other scars on my legs. And when I was leaving the camp and went to Zagreb, they took an X-ray to remove the shrapnel and then they found also a fracture from number 4, from C4 to C7. Not the vertebra itself but the joint between the vertebrae. So there was fracture of my backbone, and I was put in a plaster cast in Zagreb, a very large and solid one, for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You said that you had stitches on your head. Did you have any other kind of bandaging or anything on your head as well?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I was bandaged all over and with a net on top of the bandage. The medical kind of net to fix the bandage on my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you able to walk easily after you were hit with all the shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Both my legs were injured, and I could walk only with great difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How did your patients react to you when they saw you that way?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: They were extremely sorry when they saw me, because I had more wounds and injuries than they. Some of them even refused to be seen by me because they said I need a doctor more than they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you and the others in the atomic shelter you described to the Trial Chamber, when did you leave that shelter?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: 17 November, around 4.00 p.m. The Home Guard corps advised us that it's better to retreat to the company because the town will certainly fall. There was a lull towards the evening. All of us retreated. Some of us went to a shoe company because they had a large basement, and the others went to the warehouse of Borovo Komerc.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe that -- being told that it was better to retreat to the company. Do you mean the Borovo company?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes, the Borovo company.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you said that there was a lull towards the evening, there was a lull in what?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: There was no shooting or bombing or shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many people would you approximate were in the basement of the Borovo shoe factory?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Around 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the capacity of that basement?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: It was enough to hold 300 to 400 people at most.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you treat anyone while you were there in the basement?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes, because that night three wounded persons were brought in. They had gunshot wounds, not wounds from shells, because there were snipers around the Borovo company and they were shooting at everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you wear to identify yourself as medical personnel?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I was dressed normally, but I had a ribbon around my arm, a white ribbon, rather wide, with the sign of the Red Cross on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you the only one who wore such a band?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: No. In the shelter where I was, there were another three physicians, and in Borovo Komerc there were also three doctors. We all wore the same armband.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you leave the basement of the Borovo shoe factory?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: On the 19th, the morning of the 19th, November.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Because there was an agreement between the JNA, the Yugoslav Army on the one hand, and the homeland -- Home Guards Corps, and we were told that the army would let women, children, and medical personnel to go to Vinkovci, whereas the others would be taken prisoner. But when we got out they began separating us, men to one side, women and children to another. Without asking anyone their name or their ethnicity or anything, they started pushing us into buses using weapons, insulting us, et cetera, and they put women and children onto trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say that "they began separating us," who is -- what do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were they the only ones?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: No. There were also civilians carrying weapons and paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What, if anything, did they, meaning the JNA or paramilitaries or these civilians, did they do to the men before they were shoved onto the buses?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: They were beating them. They were saying, "Ustashas. We'll kill you." They were insulting them in all possible ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When they used the word "Ustasha," did that tell you what ethnicity they thought you were?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I had lived in Yugoslavia for a long time by that time, since 1964, and I read the history of Yugoslavia and everything. I know that there were Ustashas in Croatia before and Chetniks in Serbia before. They were nationalists. Each was concerned only about their own people. They called each other Ustashas and Chetniks. And if you want to insult a Croat, call him a murderer, then you call him Ustasha. It was during the time of the Second World War, a paramilitary or military formation these Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In your estimation how many buses were loaded with the men who had come out of the shelters?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Well, they filled the buses, and I counted nine buses, and I know exactly that I was in the fifth bus in the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did the buses go?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I saw the markings on the city buses, "Novi Sad," and I knew we were going to Serbia, to Vojvodina, and they took the road to Zrenjanin, Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On your bus were there any armed guards?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: There were two, one in the front and one in the back. I believe they were military policemen, because they had truncheons which a regular soldier doesn't have, and these men did have truncheons. So I believe they were military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What were they armed with other than truncheons?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Automatic rifles and truncheons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did they do to the prisoners on the bus?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The same. They were showering them with slurs, calling them Ustashas, saying, "We'll kill you. Keep your head down," et cetera, for no reason at all, and it went on throughout the journey.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many prisoners were on that one bus?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: More than a hundred, I believe. Literally on top of one another. More than one person per seat. We couldn't even breathe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What pace did the bus drive from Croatia to Zrenjanin, I think you said?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What pace did the buses take to get to where they were going?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: We departed around 2.30 from the Borovo company, and we arrived at Zrenjanin around a quarter to 8.00, which means we travelled more than six hours approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: As you were driving through Serb areas, were the buses greeted by people?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes, because the radio was on on the bus, and we heard war songs, and we heard announcement that a caravan of 1.200 Ustashas from Vukovar would be passing in such and such places. So in populated areas, when we were passing through there were crowds outside throwing stones, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When your bus stopped, where were you?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: We arrived at a forest. It was dark by that time. In November at 7.30, a quarter to 8.00 p.m., it's dark. Every five minutes the bus would -- one bus would stop until our turn came. We stopped by a barn, a pigsty, in fact, and we stopped about 20 to 30 metres away from that barn. When we were getting off the buses, we were passing through a gauntlet that was made up of troops, army troops, civilians and military police who were beating us with rifle butts from the moment we got off the bus until we entered the barn.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At the time that you were being beaten in this gauntlet, were you still wearing the armband you just described to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I was on the bus together with one other doctor, Dr. Karnas, and two paramedics, and Dr. Karnas said we should get out together, the four of us. And when they saw the red cross on our arms, they started shouting "These are murderers. These are people who killed our wounded to sell their organs," and they beat us even harder and tortured us even more than the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did the wounds from the shrapnel that you'd sustained, was that still obvious or had it all healed up?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The injuries were still visible because there were shrapnel wounds on my neck and there was a scar. There was the obvious stitch on the back of my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where were you hit as you were going through the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I covered my head with my hands, so I got most of the blows on my head and my back.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened once you were inside this structure, the shed -- the barn, sorry.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: It was a large door. We were supposed to sit at the entrance with our hands behind our back, head bent down, and they continued beating us for -- without any reason, without even asking our names, and that went on until all the buses were emptied. And that went on around 1.00 a.m. At 1.00 a.m., one of the prisoners who was being beaten said, "Why are you beating me? I am a Serb like you." Then they ask him, "What's your name?" And when he said his full name, then they left him proceed into the back of that barn. He was the first to have courage to say that, because there were 150 Serbs among us, and they started talking one after another. Then I raised my hand. Then they asked me who I was. I said I was a foreigner and a physician. And I was lucky because I was sitting in the middle. And they told me, "Go back. You're not a doctor, you're a mercenary." And four of them started to beat me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point did your beating stop?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: No. They were beating me. I couldn't see properly because I had to look down with my hands in the back, but the civilian approached because I could see his trousers. I could see he was a civilian, and he said, "Doctor, come with me. They won't beat you any more." At first I did not respond because I did not dare believe him. I remained sitting as I was. And he took me then under my arm, and he said, "Dr. Hicham," mentioning my name, "come with me." And then he took me to the inside part where the Serbian prisoners were, and told the others they mustn't beat me any more, and that's where I stayed until the morning alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were asked to assist with the medical needs of the prisoners in the barn?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The next morning while I was waiting there this young man who had saved me came with a lieutenant-colonel whom I later learned was called Zivanovic, and I believe he was the commander there. They were talking, and then the lieutenant-colonel came up to me and said he was sorry over what had happened to me, that there were murderers and Ustashas among us, and he said I was lucky because that person Aleksandar had seen me. He said that he was short of medical personnel, and when he got approval from Belgrade, he was supposed to set up a camp there for 300 people. He said, "Now I have more than 1.200, and can you work here as a doctor?" I said, "I could, but I can't work alone. There are other doctors among the prisoners." He said, "Let's go fetch them." So I went together with him among the prisoners. I found four other doctors and one dentist. All of us together were allocated a corner in the barn and five blankets, and he said we should set up some kind of infirmary to examine patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you or the rest of -- I'll call them your medical team, were they continue -- did they continue to beat people who were assisting you in these medical needs?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: From that moment on nobody insulted me or beat me any more, but other doctors were beaten, and the other prisoners got the same treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time turning to tab 6, 65 ter number 6395, it's a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that is a photograph that was subject of the motion to add to the 65 ter exhibit list. So with the -- I'd like to make an oral motion to add that photograph to the list. It's also part of the written motion that's been submitted to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that the written motion --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's the eighth motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The eighth one. Okay. So this is another -- another document or exhibit you want to submit to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. It's on the -- it's on our list to the Court as tab 6, but I'm just advising the Court that it hasn't been formally admitted to the 65 ter list because a motion is still outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does the Defence have a position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You say no position; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is it? The document is a photograph, you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Photograph of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I was hoping the witness would tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You would like the witness to tell. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But it's relevant to the barn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. You may add it to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time we'd ask that the witness be shown tab 6, which is 65 ter number 6395.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, directing your attention to the photograph in front of you, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Barns used for pigs, and there was this trough where we slept. That's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what name is this place known by?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd ask for admission of 65 ter number 6395.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1514, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the photograph, Dr. Malla, it looks as if those two buildings at the top of the photograph are attached. Were they in fact attached to each other?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: No, they were not attached.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what I'll describe as the long building and the short building, in which building were you?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The one that appears shorter in the picture is the same length, but you can't see it from the other building. When we arrived, we were all in the same barn. By the next day they had prepared the other part of the barn, and they moved 300 to 400 people over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you say they were all in the one barn and then moved to another. Could you indicate for us by telling us whether it's right or left? In which building did everyone gather as you described?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: In this first one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we assist the witness in marking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Malla. And is that what you mean by the first building?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the first building where we were initially accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And keeping that pen, could you indicate to the Trial Chamber where you and the others slept? And I'm now directing your attention to the inset that you described earlier.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Here in the middle was an empty space. That's where the guards were. And now you can see the troughs where some of the detainees slept, whereas the others slept on both sides on the floor next to the windows. There were no windowpanes, mind you. For the first ten days we did not have toilet facilities, so we went -- when we had to go, we did it between those people that were lying by the floor and the floor itself. Now, you can imagine when over 1.000 people did that in the barn of this size, you can imagine the conditions and the hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Malla, I'll have to be a little descriptive. Are you saying that people defecated and urinated in the same place that they slept?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. At some point, Dr. Malla, were you asked to gather statistics on the ages of the prisoners who were at the Stajicevo camp?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. Lieutenant-colonel Zivanovic asked me to prepare statistical data in terms of the age of the detainees and I did that. I prepared the statistical data. There were 19 children between the ages of 12 and 17. There were about 470 people who were over 60 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you described when you first got into the barn how you had to sit with your head bowed and your hands behind your back. What instructions did the prisoners receive about where they should look or how they could sit?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After the first day, were there any special rules for how the prisoners should conduct themselves when moving around the barn?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The detainees were not allowed to move around the barn at all. When somebody had to be interrogated, they were taken out by the guards. Otherwise, we were not allowed to move from the spot to which we were assigned. There was no moving around.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what happened if people did move around?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: They would be punished. They would be beaten. But everybody was too afraid to make a move without asking for permission. We asked for permission when we had to go to the toilet or when we wanted a drop of water to drink or when we wanted to go closer to the wall to relieve ourselves during the initial days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the floor of the barn made of?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The remains of a cement flooring. It was dirty. It was covered with pig faeces, no windowpanes. It was a barn that had been disused for 15 years. There was no electricity, no lights whatsoever, no windowpanes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened at 5.00 a.m. in the mornings while you were at the camp of Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: They got us all up, all the detainees, and they were supposed to sing the Yugoslav anthem. There's one part of the anthem that says "God damn every traitor," and they were supposed to repeat that part at least a hundred times because they were the traitors, and everybody who did not sing would be punished by being beaten. And that was what happened every day in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How often did you see or hear dogs in the Stajicevo complex?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: At first three nights in a row the civilian police came with dogs, with trained dogs, and they would let them loose into the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what did the dogs do?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: They barked at us. They ran around. But they were all muzzled. They were barking and gnarling and jumping. They caused fear among the people. It all happened in the middle of the night 3.00 or at 2.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You earlier mentioned this Lieutenant Zivanovic. Do you know whether he was a JNA or military police or something else?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: He was a member of the military police, but that military police, they were also the JNA, I believe. I am sure that they were also the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there any high-ranking military officials that you saw at the camp?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I saw three. When we first arrived there and when we suffered the most beating, there was one. There was an assistant of his. And then when I was interrogated, that was done by a major.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you know what affiliation the major had?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described to the Trial Chamber that you were no longer beaten after you were chosen to organise this medical staff. I would like to know if you were interrogated nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: There was a mistake. I was the only one who was not beaten from then on, but the other doctors, they were beaten every day. Dr. Emedi was the first one who was interrogated, one morning around 8.00. And he came back around 5.00 in the afternoon. His face was swollen. Everybody could see that he had been beaten. I spoke to him, and he said they asked him about the Croatian guards, because he treated its members. So when he couldn't answer a question, he would be beaten. I was taken out for interrogation after him, but they did not beat me, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where did the interrogations happen?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: You can't see it in this photo. There is a little wood around this complex, and there is a one-storey building which had probably been the administration building for the whole farm, because there was a hallway and five or six what probably had been offices, and in every office there was an investigator, a person who interrogated us, and we were brought there to those rooms for interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to that building. Did you -- did there come a time that you saw someone there that you knew from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: As I was coming out of the office where I was interrogated I entered the hallway. The width of that was 1 to 2 metres. There were two guards that were guarding me, and the group was coming from the other side, and I was supposed to move, and one of the guards told me Mr. Dokmanovic is coming with four escorts. And I saw him. They passed me by. And I don't think that there were more than 30 or 40 centimetres between my face and his face. He looked at me, but his eyes were empty. It was as he had never seen me before. He just passed me by. He never acknowledged me or that he knew me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And which Dokmanovic is this?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Engineer Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: He sported military trousers. That's what I could see. And a military jacket or a blouse. Some people call it a marshall jacket or an artillery jacket. In any case, it had a lot of pockets and it was a winter-type jacket. I have seen photos of Castro and Che Guevara wearing similar jackets. Some call it marshall jackets, because I believe that the marshals of the US Army wore similar jackets as part of their winter uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You said he was -- the guard told you that he was coming with four escorts. Did you see the four escorts?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I apologise. It was not the guard who told me. I saw that myself. He entered and there were four people accompanying him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: They had military uniforms, but those were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What, if any, weapons were they carrying?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: They were armed, yes. They had automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How did you feel when Slavko Dokmanovic looked you in the eyes and ignored you?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I was very disappointed. First of all, he had been my friend, my family friend. We had known each other for a long time. Second of all, he knew I was a doctor. I treated his father when he was sick, and I didn't have to, because I worked at the Borovo company. I was not a -- his father's doctor. He knew that during the war I was a doctor who treated everybody. I was not a defendant. I never carried weapons. And in my view, he was in such a position that he could have helped me to get out of there. He could have said that I was a doctor who didn't have to be there, but he pretended that he had never seen me before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we're going to hopefully play some clips. Turning now to tab 5, which is 65 ter number 48 -- I'll change the order, in fact. Instead, turning to tab 14, 65 ter number 4886.2. And that is an extract from 8 minute 58 seconds to 12 minute 32 seconds, and coming from Rule 65 ter 4886, but we'll start at 11 minute, 14 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, what is the question? What is the foundation for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would like to play it for the witness and see if he recognises the people or person depicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my view it is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could now -- and I see that the time code is at 11 minute 12 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Today Borovo Naselje is the most destroyed and deserted town on the entire planet. We are talking to Slavko Dokmanovic about that. What are we supposed to do? "Unfortunately, Vukovar indeed is the most destroyed city on the entire polity. A city which used to be clean, which used to have peace and order is no longer. We will do everything to restore the city. We're working on this very intensively in two directions. First of all, we're going to organise the civilian authorities, and that will be done today or perhaps tomorrow. Preparations to clean up the city and to rebuild it again depend on several matters. Firstly, it is necessary to improve sanitary conditions, then we'll clean up the rubble, and after that we will build a new city according to an existing project. I sincerely hope that this new city will never be an Ustasha city but a real Serbian city where all people will live free."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, before you is a freeze-frame from this video-clip, and the time code is 11 minute, 24 seconds. Do you recognise the person in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. That's Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is what he is wearing similar to or different from what you saw him wearing at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: It's different.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd move for the admission of 65 ter number 4486.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object at this point. For the purpose of identification of Mr. Dokmanovic, vide-clip is enough, not the whole text of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's -- we would like to admit the clip for the substance of what Mr. Dokmanovic is saying, but the witness has identified the speaker as being someone he knows and who is indeed Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The witness did not say anything about the substance of his statement in this video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's because the clip speaks for itself and he doesn't need to. He just needs to identify the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, was that -- when you saw Dokmanovic at Stajicevo, was that the first time you had seen him in a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: No. That was the second time. The first time was around the 5th of August in Trpinja. I went there to help a friend's son. She called me. I was there, and on returning to the centre of Trpinja, I saw him. He saw me. He asked me to have a cup of coffee with him, but I turned him down because it was already late. He was wearing a uniform of the JNA reserve. The trousers and the shirt that he was wearing at the time were olive-drab colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, we have about, if I'm correct, about seven minutes left, and what I'd like to do is to ask you to describe the people -- or the prisoners that you treated in -- in the barn. My first question in this regard, in fact, is: Were their prisoners who upon their arrival in Stajicevo already were not able to walk?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. Among the civilians there, there was an elderly man who was paralysed. Among the civilians there was also a man with a catheter, also an elderly man. There were two old men with crutches.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you know these people personally?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: I knew one personally but not the others. That one was from Borovo Naselje, but I was not their GP. I was only a company doctor, and they no longer worked there. They were too old to be workers of that company.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The prisoners that you treated were -- had some of them already been wounded upon their arrival at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: There were a lot of wounded. They needed to have their wounds dressed. They needed therapy. But every day somebody else was wounded as a result of beating. There were seven people among some elderly men whose ribs were fractured when they had to run the gauntlet of rifle butts and sticks. That's when they were injured, when their ribs were broken.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you treated these people did they tell you how they had got injured, for example, when they had broken ribs?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that they had been beaten and that their broken ribs were a result of that. I mean, it is -- it was really incomprehensible. They were not all Croats. Some of them were Serbs. There was an elderly man of some 70 years of age. His ribs were fractured. He was a Serb. I can even tell you what his family name was. He hailed from the Jeftic family. His grandson, Jeftic, was one of the detainees in the camp. He couldn't breathe. He wanted to be transported to the hospital to be treated there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did they tell you why they were beaten? For example, let me restrict my question to the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Listen, initially when both the Croats and the Serbs were beaten it was nothing but pure hatred. Okay, when there is a war there is a war, but if somebody's detained, you cannot let rip on him. And then people were interrogated, and they were beaten. They called them traitors. If they had stayed behind in Borovo and Vukovar, they thought that they had fought against them, they called them traitors, and they would beat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One clarifying question because we're close to the end, you said: "... they were beaten. They called them traitors. If they had stayed behind in Borovo and Vukovar, they thought that they had fought against them." Who was considered to be a traitor? It's unclear for the record.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Listen, as far as I know, there was a small number of Serbs who were members of the Croatian guards, and they fought together with them. They were civilians who didn't want to leave Vukovar -- or Borovo Naselje. They wanted to stay in their homes, and they were considered traitors because they remained living with the enemy and it was a given that they had collaborated with their enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I see, Your Honours. May I ask just one question to clear the records before we leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You said they wanted to stay in their homes. Are you talking about Serbs or Croats when you say that?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA
utterances.text: Both Serbs and Croats, but there were also Serbs that didn't want to leave. They wanted to stay in their homes. They didn't want to move.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Malla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, this is the end of the hearing today. You will come back at 9.00 tomorrow morning. I remind you that you are under oath, which means that you are not allowed in the meantime to discuss your testimony with anybody, and you are not allowed to talk to any the parties. The court usher will escort you out of court, and we'll see you tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 12th day of April, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
